name: Obetrol (amphetamine salts)
lead: Obetrol was a prescription diet pill sold in the United States from 1960 until its approval was withdrawn in 1973. It combined four amphetamine and methamphetamine salts, and it was used to help people lose weight by reducing appetite alongside a lower-calorie diet, the same fat-loss goal that drives cutting in looksmaxxing today.[1][2]

The original 10 mg tablet reportedly held 2.5 mg each of methamphetamine saccharate, methamphetamine hydrochloride, racemic amphetamine sulfate and dextroamphetamine sulfate, with a 20 mg version doubling the amounts.[1] The FDA approved the formula in January 1960 and withdrew approval in September 1973, citing weak supporting research.[1]

Rexar later dropped the methamphetamine salts, and after Richwood Pharmaceuticals acquired Rexar in 1993 the reformulated product was renamed Adderall, which was approved for ADHD in February 1996.[1] No drug marketed as Obetrol exists today, but amphetamine-class appetite suppression is still discussed in physique forums, and a 1966 journal paper compared Obetrol with diet therapy and phenmetrazine for weight loss.[1][3][4]

chain: Lower calorie intake alongside a reduced diet
angle.text: Obetrol was prescribed to reduce appetite so patients could keep to a lower-calorie diet and lose weight. Its present-day relevance to looks is mostly historical, as the forerunner of amphetamine-based appetite suppression that some physique-focused users still discuss.

infobox: Not marketed; amphetamines are US Schedule II

paras: Obetrol was indicated for exogenous obesity as an aid to reducing appetite alongside a lower-calorie diet.[1][2] Grokipedia adds that doctors also used it off-label for attention problems in children before ADHD was formally defined; this comes from an AI-generated page.[2]

The appearance rationale was straightforward: amphetamines reduce appetite, so a patient eating less could lose body fat and look slimmer. Amphetamine-class drugs of this period were prescribed on that logic, and appetite loss and weight loss remain listed among the common effects of the descendant product Adderall.[9][1]

As a mixture of amphetamine and methamphetamine salts, Obetrol acted as a central nervous system stimulant, and appetite suppression was the effect for which it was prescribed.[1][2] Systematic reviews of amphetamine salts in ADHD report that they are among the best-supported ADHD medications but are associated with side effects such as hypertension and, in rare cases, psychotic symptoms.[5] A JACC review of stimulant ADHD therapies reported modest increases in resting heart rate and blood pressure, with case reports of arrhythmia and other cardiac events that were not shown to be causal.[6]

A 1966 report in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society compared weight losses under three regimens: diet therapy, phenmetrazine, and an amphetamine combination (Obetrol).[3] Beyond that, no modern trials of Obetrol itself were found. Later research on amphetamine salts concerns ADHD and stimulant-use disorders rather than weight loss.[5][6]

The 1966 comparison in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society is the one weight-loss study in which Obetrol is named, and it set the amphetamine combination against diet therapy and phenmetrazine.[3] The FDA's 1973 withdrawal rested on the finding that the data submitted for the combination were poorly controlled and did not test the ingredients individually.[1]

Rexar developed the product after wartime and postwar medical adoption of amphetamines, and marketed it during the era of widespread amphetamine diet-pill prescribing.[1][2] A 1970 FDA order required new applications for amphetamine products, and in September 1973 the agency withdrew Obetrol's approval, citing weak research evidence of efficacy.[1] Grokipedia also links the withdrawal to rising concern about amphetamine misuse during the period known as the speed epidemic.[2] Rexar moved production to Valley Stream, New York, and Richwood acquired it in 1993; the FDA issued a warning in 1994 before Adderall's ADHD approval in 1996.[1]

According to Wikipedia, the product was first made by Obetrol Pharmaceuticals in Brooklyn, New York, in the 1950s, later became a division of Rexar Pharmacal, which moved to Valley Stream, New York, before 1972. Wholesalers received it as Obetrol while physicians received it as Oby-Rex. The original tablets were blue (10 mg) and orange (20 mg) and stamped "OP".[1]

The FDA approved the formula on 19 January 1960. In 1970 it required new applications for previously approved amphetamine products and treated an amphetamine and methamphetamine mixture as a combination drug whose ingredients had to be shown effective and safe individually and together. In September 1973 it withdrew Obetrol's approval under the Drug Efficacy Study Implementation programme, saying the submitted research was vague, poorly controlled and did not test the individual ingredients.[1]

Because the FDA treated a methamphetamine-free blend of amphetamine and dextroamphetamine salts as a single entity, Rexar kept selling that version under the Obetrol name. After Richwood Pharmaceuticals of Florence, Kentucky, acquired Rexar in 1993 it was renamed Adderall and marketed for attention-deficit disorder; the FDA issued a warning in 1994, Richwood resubmitted it, and approval for ADHD came on 13 February 1996. Richwood merged with Shire in 1995, and the Adderall name later passed to Barr Pharmaceuticals, which Teva acquired in 2008.[1]

Grokipedia reports advertisements in the late 1960s and early 1970s promising rapid weight loss, and describes the drug as part of the broader amphetamine diet-pill era.[2] Obetrol now appears mostly as a historical forerunner of Adderall.

On T Nation, users who ask about appetite suppressants for lean-out phases mention a range of stimulants, and others in the community point out that mixed amphetamine salts are a different drug from methamphetamine.[7][8]

Wikipedia describes the drug as popular in the 1950s and 1960s and reports that Andy Warhol used it as his recreational drug of choice. David Foster Wallace's novel The Pale King features a character who abuses Obetrol, and the book's slang terms include "obetrolling" and "doubling".[1]

Adderall, the successor, is a Schedule II controlled substance in the United States, Schedule I in Canada and Class B in the UK. Wikipedia notes that performance-enhancing and recreational uses are illegal in many countries, and lists cardiovascular effects, insomnia and, with heavy misuse, psychosis among its documented adverse effects.[9]

card.summary: The 1960s amphetamine-and-methamphetamine diet pill that became Adderall's ancestor.
card.note: Approval withdrawn in 1973; contained amphetamine and methamphetamine salts.

quick.overview:
Obetrol was a brand-name US prescription pill from the 1950s-60s that combined amphetamine and methamphetamine salts for weight loss. It was approved in 1960 and its approval was withdrawn in 1973.

Its later methamphetamine-free reformulation became Adderall, approved for ADHD in 1996.
quick.mechanism: As a stimulant mixture, it suppressed appetite through the central nervous system effects typical of amphetamines.
quick.risks: Amphetamines carry misuse and cardiovascular concerns, and the 1973 withdrawal cited weak efficacy evidence as well as the speed-epidemic context. It is no longer sold.
